p: Two Tuesdays went by without Kit bringing Vern her one sentence. He asked once, and then he let it be.

On the March drill her assistant crew chief, Fisk, came in off a night at the warehouse, and Kit gave him a wheel change on two two eight anyway. The forms said the wheel was torqued, with his initials. At the tool crib she found the torque wrench had never left its hook.

She held the jet first and wrote it up. Then she walked Fisk to the far side of the jet, where nobody could hear, and they torqued the wheel together. He owned the radio call too, the one where he'd said the forms were done. He hadn't told her he was worn out, he said, because she'd have pulled him, and then she'd know.

She took him straight to Boyd and let him tell it himself. Boyd took him off torque tasks until Kit retrains him and sent it up the line in writing. When Boyd asked about Fisk's night shift, Kit said she'd seen it at four and let it go. Boyd said that was how he'd want the shop run when he's gone.

That afternoon Kit read one of Vern's old logs, the first one where he'd written MY MISS. She thought about her own 2019 score sheet, folded under the foam in her toolbox, and how she'd always said it was Boyd's.

She got her test voucher at the base test office, in the building where she'd sat the test in 2019, and said no to the room at the end of the hall. That night she told Graham the whole day, her own part included, and booked the test herself: Saturday, May 15, at eight in the morning, in Kansas City. She wiped the question mark off Graham's whiteboard, and in the morning he texted that he'd drive.

On Sunday she gave the safety brief as her own miss and left Fisk's name out of it. In the heritage room Vern ran her through a timed analogy block in test order. Down the margin she'd written thirty eight minutes for reading, the old paper test's number. She guessed the last three, and her hands were flat on the table. Vern told her she'd sat it before.
Leon Yates. The night lead at the Tolliver water plant, sixty one.
Patrice Pruett. Vern's wife of fifty one years, a retired librarian.

She did Vern's twenty five word problems in twenty seven of the twenty nine minutes, and he marked them with his pencil while she sat across from him with her coat still on. Nineteen right. He wrote the number at the top of the first page and went through the six she'd missed one at a time, slow, as if nothing else had been said in that room all afternoon. Two were rates where she'd mixed up minutes and hours. He circled those twice.
At five he locked the heritage room. Out in the lot he said Tuesday, and she said Tuesday.

Then she drove back across the ramp to the shop, which was dark except for the light over the coffee, and opened her toolbox. She lifted the shadow board foam out by one corner, the way you'd lift a floor mat looking for a spare key. The papers were where they'd been for seven years, soft at the creases. She took the top one and put the foam back down over the rest. Then she buttoned the sheet into the inside pocket of her coat and drove to the plant for an eleven o'clock shift.
Vern's Nav Table: rates, and describing yourself.
One sentence under every rate problem.
Thirty one years in dispatch, and nearly every number I signed was a rate times a time. Fuel, a front moving east, a crew's duty day. The airplanes changed every few years. That sentence never did.

Arithmetic Reasoning is twenty five word problems in twenty nine minutes, five choices apiece, with scratch paper. I couldn't tell you for certain whether a calculator's allowed, so practice like it isn't. That works out to a little over a minute a problem, and most of your minute goes to reading the thing and setting it up. The arithmetic's usually the short part.

A lot of them are rate problems in a different shirt. Underneath every one is the same sentence, amount equals rate times time. Fuel burned is burn rate times hours. Miles is speed times time. Gallons is gallons a minute times minutes. Got two of the three, you've got the third: amount over rate gives you the time, amount over time gives you the rate.

I wrote the units next to every number on my nav log for twenty years, and I'd tell you to do the same on scratch paper. Pounds over pounds a minute leaves you minutes. If what's left over doesn't match what they asked for, you set it up wrong, and you found out for free.
How the exam asks it. Before you calculate, name the three pieces in your head. Whichever one they're asking for is the one you don't have.

Two rates only compare when they're per the same thing. Twenty one drops in three minutes and twenty four in six sound close. Per minute they're seven and four, and the first is three quarters faster. Put both on the same clock before you decide anything.

Clocks are where most of the misses live. An hour isn't a hundred minutes. Three hours and forty minutes isn't 3.4 hours. It's three and two thirds. Turn hours and minutes into minutes, or into a fraction of an hour you can work with: fifteen minutes is a quarter, twenty is a third, forty five is three quarters.
Watch which way a rate points. Gallons a day and days per gallon are upside down from each other. Before you divide, ask which one the question is holding.
How the exam asks it. When a time is in hours and minutes, convert it before you multiply. Five hours thirty six minutes is 5.6 hours, not 5.36.

Some problems change the rate in the middle. A truck runs one stretch at one speed and the rest at another. A tank fills fast until it's nearly full and then slow. Cut the problem where the rate changes, work each piece on its own, and add the pieces.

Don't average the two rates unless each one ran for the same length of time. Forty five miles an hour and sixty average out to fifty two and a half, and that's only right if the truck spent equal time at each. Usually it didn't, and the averaged number can be sitting right there among the five choices.
How the exam asks it. If a choice is the average of two rates from the problem, check whether the times were equal before you take it.

Kit's plant runs a rate problem every shift. Pounds of chlorine a day equals the dose in milligrams per liter, times the flow in million gallons a day, times 8.34. The 8.34 is what a gallon of water weighs in pounds, and it turns a strength and a flow into a weight you could set on a scale.

You won't see that formula on the test. You'll see its shape a dozen times: a rate, times an amount, times one number that makes the units come out. The wrong choices tend to be the right formula with one piece left off, or with a decimal slid over a place.
It runs backward, too. Know the pounds and the flow and you can divide to get the dose. A formula with three parts in it is three different problems, depending on which part they hide from you.
How the exam asks it. If a choice is yours times ten or a hundred, check your decimal before you check anything else.

Plenty of wrong choices on this subtest are real numbers from the problem, answering a question nobody asked. The drops counted, not the rate. What's left after three loads, not how far short the plan was. Before you pick, read the last sentence again and say back what it wants.
Round first, and see where the answer has to land. 1.8 times 2.1 times 8.34 is about 4 times 8, so somewhere near 32. If you get 320 or 3.2, you don't need to check the arithmetic to know.
Scores are built from the number you get right, with no penalty for a wrong one, so a guess costs you nothing. If a problem is eating your minute, take your best estimate and move on.
How the exam asks it. Estimate before you calculate. A rough answer often rules out two or three of the five.

After the break comes the Self-Description Inventory, 240 statements in 45 minutes on the current Pearson page. Each one says something about how you work or deal with people, and you mark how well it fits you on a five point scale: strongly disagree, moderately disagree, neither agree nor disagree, moderately agree, strongly agree.

It isn't graded, and in the 2015 pamphlet it feeds no composite. The pamphlet says it's there to match you with Air Force work that people who answer like you find satisfying, so a faked answer only points you at the wrong job. There are no right answers, and nobody can coach you to one. Answer as yourself, as you are now, not as the officer you think they're hoping for. Go fast, about eleven seconds a statement, and take the first honest answer. Answer the way you would on any other day of the week.

Pearson's page says each question must be answered to receive results, so don't leave any blank. And don't spend the forty five minutes trying to work out what each line is for. That's about the only way to do this one badly.
How the exam asks it. On the inventory, take your first honest answer and keep moving. Thinking longer doesn't make an answer truer.
Every rendezvous I ever worked was two airplanes and a clock. Where are they, how fast is the gap closing, and when do I tell the pilot to turn.

Same sentence as the top of this page, in a flight suit. Distance equals rate times time, d rt. Miles an hour times hours gives miles. Knots times hours gives nautical miles, because a knot is one nautical mile an hour and that's all a knot is. Turn it around and time is distance over rate. Get every piece on the same clock and the same kind of mile first. Sixty knots is a nautical mile a minute, the handiest fact I own. Thirty miles an hour is 44 feet a second, since a mile is 5,280 feet and an hour is 3,600 seconds. Don't memorize that one. Know which way to multiply.

Two things moving changes one piece, the rate. Coming at each other or flying apart, add the speeds. That's closing speed. Going the same way, one catching the other, take the slow one from the fast one. The distance is the gap when the clock starts. Here's one shaped like the ones I worked. Tanker at 310 knots, receiver head on at 370, 136 nautical miles apart. They close at 680 knots. 136 over 680 is a fifth of an hour, which is 12 minutes. I'd have had the tanker turning well before that, but the arithmetic's the arithmetic.

Overtaking has a wrinkle, the head start. Whoever left first already has some road behind them, and that's your gap. Work the gap out, then divide it by the difference in speeds. The misses: adding the speeds when they're going the same way, so somebody catches up faster than either one is driving. Writing 12 minutes as 0.12 of an hour. I watched a lieutenant do that on a fuel plan in 1988 and miss by most of a tank.

Average speed is total distance over total time. Nothing else. Say the drive to Kansas City goes 36 miles of river road at 45, then 84 miles of interstate at 70. The river road takes 0.8 of an hour, 48 minutes. The interstate takes 1.2 hours. That's 120 miles in 2 hours, an average of 60. Average the two speeds instead and you get 57 and a half, and 57.5 can be sitting in the choices. You spend more of that trip at 70 than at 45, so the true average leans toward 70.

Try one. The plant's sampling truck leaves at 9:00 doing 40. Gene follows at 9:15 doing 55. When does he catch it? The truck's 10 miles out by 9:15, Gene gains 15 miles an hour, and 10 over 15 is two thirds of an hour. 9:55. If you said 9:40, you forgot he left a quarter hour late.
How the exam asks it. Toward each other or apart, add the speeds. Same way, subtract. Average speed is total miles over total hours, never the average of the speeds.

A ratio is a comparison, and you'll see it written three ways: 3 to 2, 3:2, or three halves. A proportion is two ratios set equal. When one piece is missing, cross multiply. Line them up, centimeters across from centimeters, miles across from miles, and multiply corner to corner.

Map and scale problems are proportions with a ruler. One plotting chart I carried in the nineties ran 2 centimeters to 15 nautical miles. Say a leg measures 11 centimeters. Write it 2 over 15 equals 11 over x, centimeters on top both times. Cross multiply: 2x is 165, so x is 82.5 nautical miles. The miss is flipping one side, 2 over 15 equals x over 11, which gets you about 1.5. That's a long line on the chart and a mile and a half out the window. A longer line is more miles. Never fewer.

Some go the other way, and that's inverse proportion. More pumps, fewer hours. Faster truck, less time. Higher feed, the chemical runs out sooner. When doubling one halves the other, the product stays put instead of the ratio. Say the plant had a 720 gallon tank, thirty days of it at 24 gallons a day. Gene raises the feed to 32 a day. 720 over 32 is 22 and a half days. Set it up straight, 24 over 30 equals 32 over x, and you'd get 40 days. More chemical a day lasting longer ought to make you laugh before it makes you circle it.

"Parts to" splits are a common setup. Add the parts, divide the total by that, and you've got one part. Say Kit split Graham's 66 hours eight parts to three, arithmetic to words. Eleven parts, so 6 hours a part. Arithmetic gets 48, words get 18. The miss is dividing 66 by 8 and calling that the arithmetic, or stopping at the 6 because it came out so clean. A part isn't an answer. Multiply it back out, then add your pieces and make sure Graham's 66 comes back.

Try one. Gene's got a mix sheet taped over the day tank in his own hand: two and a half pounds of soda ash to every 10 gallons of water. Kit's filling it to 36 gallons. How much soda ash? Nine pounds. Get 144 and you flipped a side. Gene'd come in Monday to a tank of paste.
How the exam asks it. Same units in the same spot on both sides, then cross multiply. Then ask yourself, bigger or smaller than what I started with? Know that before you look at the choices.

Percent means per hundred, so 35 percent is 35 over 100, or 0.35. Nearly every percent problem is one sentence: the part is the percent times the whole. My sixth grade teacher had it on the board all year: of means times, is means equals. 35 percent of 240 is 0.35 times 240, which is 84. Is what percent of? That's part over whole. 27 is what percent of 180? 27 over 180 is 0.15, so 15 percent.

Percent change is the change over where you started. Not where you ended up. Say the plant's power bill went from $2,400 to $2,760. That's up $360, and 360 over 2,400 is 15 percent. Now say it came back down to $2,400 the next month. Same $360, but it's over 2,760 now, so about 13 percent. Same dollars, two percents, because the base moved. The miss is dividing by the new number, so expect that one in the choices.

That's why up 10 percent and then down 10 percent doesn't land you back home. Up 10 is times 1.1. Down 10 is times 0.9, and that second 10 percent comes off the bigger number. 1.1 times 0.9 is 0.99. You finish 1 percent under where you started, whatever you started with. Two raises of 20 percent go the other way: 1.2 times 1.2 is 1.44, a 44 percent raise, not 40. Chain the multipliers. Never add the percents.

Patrice kept the savings book in our house for fifty years, and she'd tell you this part. Simple interest is the principal, times the rate, times the years. $1,500 at 3 percent for 4 years earns 1,500 times 0.03 times 4, $180, and the interest never earns anything of its own. Compound interest pays interest on the interest. $1,500 at 3 percent compounded yearly is $1,545 after one year and $1,591.35 after two. Simple would have you at $1,590. That dollar thirty five is the whole difference, early on. Watch "earns" against "worth." One wants the interest. The other wants the interest plus what you put in.

Discount, markup and sales tax are one move. A discount takes a percent off, so multiply by what's left. A markup or a tax puts one on, so multiply by one plus it. A cordless drill at the hardware store lists for $120 at 15 percent off. You pay 85 percent of it, $102. Sales tax at 6 percent goes on what you're paying, so $102 times 1.06, $108.12. A store that paid $80 for a socket set and marked it up 35 percent put it on the shelf at $108. If they give you the shelf price and ask what the store paid, divide by 1.35. Taking 35 percent off the shelf price gets you $70.20, and that's wrong.
Try one. A $90 tool bag is 30 percent off, and tax is 5 percent. You pay $66.15. If you got $67.50, you took off 25 percent, 30 less 5. A tax and a discount don't cancel like that.
How the exam asks it. Percent change goes over the starting number. Successive changes multiply. They don't add.

We mixed nothing on a tanker but fuel and coffee, and I got the coffee wrong for twenty years. A mixture problem tracks one thing, the pure stuff. Concentration times volume tells you how much of it is in there, and water poured in doesn't add any.

Say a drum of hypochlorite comes at 12.5 percent, and Gene wants some of it cut to 10. Start with 12 gallons. The pure chemical in it is 12 times 0.125, 1.5 gallons. That 1.5 has to be 10 percent of the new batch, so the batch is 15 gallons. Add 3 gallons of water. The miss is answering 15. That's the batch, not what you poured.

Blending two strengths, write the pure stuff for each and set the totals equal. Thirty gallons at 6 percent plus x gallons at 15 makes 30 plus x gallons at 9. So 1.8 plus 0.15x equals 2.7 plus 0.09x. Then 0.06x is 0.9, and x is 15. Nine sits closer to 6 than to 15, so there's more of the weak one, two to one. The other miss is averaging the percents. A batch leans toward whichever strength it has more of.

Working together is a rate problem in a different shirt again. Anyone who does a job in 5 hours does a fifth of it an hour. Rates add. Times don't. Say the plant has two pumps on one clearwell. One fills it in 5 hours and the other in 20. Their combined rate is a fifth plus a twentieth, five twentieths, a quarter of the tank an hour. So 4 hours. Check it the dumb way: two pumps have to beat the faster pump alone, so anything over 5 is out. Average the times and you get 12 and a half. Add them and you get 25. Both make good wrong choices.

Fill and drain is the same thing with a minus in it. A drain works against you, so its rate comes off. An inlet that fills a tank in 3 hours, with a drain that would empty it in 15, puts in a third an hour and loses a fifteenth. Five fifteenths less one is four fifteenths an hour. Flip it: 15 over 4, 3.75 hours, which is 3 hours 45 minutes. If the drain's as quick as the fill or quicker, the tank never fills, and a practice test might ask that.

Try two. How many gallons of water turn 8 gallons of 15 percent into 6 percent? Twelve. The pure part is 1.2 gallons, which makes 20 gallons at 6 percent, so you add 12 to the 8. And Kit can safety wire a row of fasteners in 30 minutes, Fisk in 45. Together it's 18 minutes, since a thirtieth plus a forty fifth is five ninetieths, an eighteenth of the job a minute.

How the exam asks it. In a mixture, track the pure part. Working together, add the rates, never the times. When both are helping, the answer beats the faster one alone. With a drain, it's slower than the fill alone.

Most of the twenty five look like something on this page already. The rest are a handful of old chestnuts that were in arithmetic books before I could read one. Learn the move for each and they go quick.

Averaging two groups. When the groups aren't the same size, the bigger one pulls harder. Multiply each average by its head count, add those up, and divide by everybody. Fisk's warehouse runs two crews on nights. Six pickers average 72 pallets a shift, and fourteen average 82. That's 432 pallets plus 1,148, so 1,580 pallets over 20 people, an average of 79. The miss is splitting the difference and calling it 77. That only works when the crews are the same size. It's the same trap as averaging two speeds.

Simple probability. The chance of a thing is the ways it can happen over all the ways anything can happen. I keep a coffee can of loose screws in the den, forty years of fixing things I should've paid somebody to fix. Say it's 7 wood screws, 5 machine screws and 8 drywall screws. Reach in blind, and the chance of a machine screw is 5 over 20, a quarter. Anything but a machine screw is 1 less that, three quarters. Put it back and draw again, and two machine screws in a row is a quarter times a quarter, a sixteenth. The miss is 5 over 15, machine screws over the other screws. The bottom number is everything in the can, the 5 included.

Two groups that overlap. Some people are in both, and if you just add the groups you count them twice. Start with everybody and take out the ones in neither. What's left is the people in at least one. Whatever the two groups add up to past that is the overlap. Gene's plant has 12 people. Eight hold a treatment license, 5 hold a commercial driver's license, and 2 hold neither. So 10 hold at least one. Eight plus 5 is 13, and 13 less 10 is 3 who hold both. The miss is forgetting the 2 with neither, taking 12 from 13, and answering 1. Draw two circles that overlap if it helps. I still do.

Handshakes and pairings. Every pair once is each person times everybody else, cut in half, because me shaking your hand is the same shake as you shaking mine. That's n times n less 1, over 2. Eleven of my old crew turned up at a reunion in Omaha a few years back, and every one of us shook every other one's hand. Eleven times 10 is 110, halved, 55 handshakes. The miss is stopping at 110, which counts every handshake twice. The same move tells you how many games in a league where everybody plays everybody once.

Two prices and a total. Two unknowns need two sentences, one for the count and one for the money. Patrice's church sold 30 pies and loaves at the spring sale and took in $236. Pies were $10 and loaves $6. Call the pies p, so the loaves are 30 less p. Then 10p plus 6 times 30 less p is 236. That's 4p plus 180 equals 236, so 4p is 56 and p is 14. Fourteen pies, 16 loaves, and $140 plus $96 is $236. There's a quick way too. If all 30 had been loaves, that's $180, $56 short. Each pie swapped in adds $4, and 56 over 4 is 14. The miss is answering 16, the loaves, when they asked for pies.

Consecutive integers. Call the first one n. Plain consecutive numbers step by 1: n, n plus 1, n plus 2. Consecutive odd numbers step by 2, and so do consecutive even ones, which is the part people get backward. Say four consecutive odd numbers add up to 72. That's n plus n plus 2 plus n plus 4 plus n plus 6, or 4n plus 12, equals 72. So 4n is 60, n is 15, and the numbers are 15, 17, 19 and 21. Quicker: 72 over 4 is 18, the middle, and the four odd numbers sitting around 18 are those same four. Step by 1 instead and n comes out 16.5. A fraction where a whole number belongs means the setup's wrong.

Age problems. The gap between two ages never changes. Write each age at the time the problem names, years ago or years from now, and move both people the same number of years. Our tankers are older than most of the kids who crew them, so here's one with a jet in it. Say the jet's got 39 years on its airman. Eight years back it was 4 times the airman's age. Call the airman's age back then x. The jet was x plus 39 back then, and they told you that's 4x. So 3x is 39 and x is 13. Put the 8 years back and the airman's 21 now, the jet 60. The miss is answering 13, the age eight years ago, or taking the 8 years off only one of them.

Train length plus platform. A train hasn't cleared a bridge till its last car is off, so the engine goes the bridge plus the whole train behind it. There's a freight runs the river line past the plant, and I've sat at that crossing more nights than I'd like. Call it 1,320 feet of cars doing 30 miles an hour over a 660 foot bridge. Thirty miles an hour is 44 feet a second, from the top of this page. The front has to go 660 plus 1,320, which is 1,980 feet, and 1,980 over 44 is 45 seconds. Answer 15 and you only counted the bridge. Answer 30 and you only counted the train. A signal post? Just the train. The post's no wider than my thumb.

How the exam asks it. Most misses on these are somebody counted twice, or an answer to the wrong question. The loaves when they asked about pies. How old the airman was back then. The bridge without the train.

Monday, March 8, twenty to three in the morning, and the residual alarm went off. At the Tolliver plant that's a two note beep and a yellow box on the screen that says LOW RESIDUAL CLEARWELL. No horn. Nobody'd hear it from the lot, and at that hour nobody's in the lot. Yates, the night lead, was down at the river intake with a flashlight, cussing at the screen down there for packing up with leaves again. He did that most nights in March.
Point nine nine leaving the plant. They liked it around one four, and the alarm was set at one even. She got up, and the sheet in her coat crackled, and she let it.

Chemical room, end of the hall. The hypo pump's a gray plastic box on the wall about the size of a lunch pail, over a drum of the stuff. Hypochlorite. Call it bleach if you want, it's just a lot meaner than what's under your sink. The pump was clicking along like it was any other night. Click, green light, click, green light. The clear tube from the drum up to it was full of little bubbles, though, all the way up. And the line out the other side, the one to the injection point, wasn't going anywhere.
The pump is stroking and the line isn't moving. What's wrong with it?
A. The bleach got cold in the night and went too thick to pull.
B. Something's clogged downstream, and the stroke can't push past it.
C. The drum ran dry, and the pump's been pulling on air.
D. Gas in the pump head, squeezing instead of pushing the liquid.

Bucket from under the sink. She held it under the priming valve on the pump head and cracked the valve a quarter turn, and it spat at her, foam and a burp of gas and then yellow. The clicking got heavy. You could hear it. She shut the valve. Boyd always said don't walk off from a thing the second it starts working, so she gave it another minute, standing there at three in the morning with a bucket of bleach foam, till the line was yellow all the way to the wall.

That'll hold, Sergeant. I learned this one in Guam, standing behind a crew chief who was bleeding a brake line at three in the morning. He called every bubble by name, and none of the names would go in a log. "Air squashes," he told me. "Fluid don't. That's the whole lesson." Your pump's got the same disease. Bleach is always coming apart a little and gassing off, the gas rides up into the pump head, and then the pump's squeezing a bubble all night and calling it work.
Decision two. The last good number.

Back at the console she pulled up the night's readings, every half hour since midnight, the way the plant printed them for the log. What she was after was the last good number before the drop. That'd tell her how long the town's water had gone out light.

Readings every half hour from midnight to three. Plant flow, in million gallons a day: one point two six, one point two five, one point two five, one point two four, one point two five, one point two five, one point two six. Chlorine residual, in milligrams per liter: one point four two, one point four one, one point four oh, one point three eight, one point two one, one point oh six, point nine four. Feed pump, percent: forty eight at every reading.
What does the residual row read at 0130?
A. Read 1.24, the row above it under 0130.
B. Read 1.21, the residual row under 0200.
C. Read 1.38, the residual row under 0130.
D. Read 1.40, the residual row under 0100.

Finger on 0130, finger on the residual row: 1.38. Then the neighbors, so she'd know what a slip would have looked like. 1.40 before it, 1.21 after, and 1.24 up in the flow row. So the pump had quit a little after half past one, and the water had gone out light for the better part of two hours. The bottom row said 48 percent all night. The pump had reported what it was told to do, not what it did.

Right. Log it. Row, then column, then a look around the cell. On the test many of the wrong choices sit right next to the answer. And notice that bottom row. The pump said forty eight all night long. A gauge that shows you the setting isn't showing you the flow. I've been lied to by better instruments than that one.

The log had a line for chlorine fed, in pounds a day, and the night's was hers to fill in. March's dose was 2.4 milligrams per liter; Gene had set it on the first. The plant was making 1.25 million gallons a day.

Everybody at the plant knew the pounds formula the way they knew the gate code. Milligrams per liter, times million gallons a day, times 8.34, which is what a gallon of water weighs. Every line above hers in the log said 25.0, the same number night after night in four different handwritings. She worked it anyway, on the back of the clipboard. A number somebody else wrote down was somebody else's arithmetic.
What does the formula give for the night's line in the log?
A. 20.02 pounds a day: 2.4 times 8.34, flow left out.
C. 3 pounds a day: 2.4 times 1.25, and that's all.
D. 250.2 pounds a day: 2.4 times 1.25 times 83.4.

2.4 times 1.25 is 3, the friendly kind of number. Three times 8.34 is 25.02. She wrote 25.0 on the line like everybody else. Then in the remarks she started on the rest: what the pump had actually done between half past one and a quarter after three, which wasn't 25 of anything.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Strength, times flow, times what a gallon weighs. The 8.34 is what turns milligrams per liter and millions of gallons into pounds you could lift. Every wrong choice here is that formula with one piece dropped or a decimal slid, which is how a lot of wrong choices get built. Round it first. Two and a half times one and a quarter is about three, three eights is twenty four, so the answer lives near twenty five.

Yates came back up from the intake at half past three with river mud on his boots and wet leaves stuck to the knees of his coveralls. He was sixty one and had worked nights at the plant since before Kit could drive. He read the screen over her shoulder, then the remarks she'd started, and pulled out the other chair.

Leave that out. She asked him why. It came back. Never got anywhere near the floor. He rubbed his eyes with the heels of his hands. And it's the third time this month. I primed it twice on my nights and kept it out of the book. You write tonight's, and Gene reads it at the huddle and asks why it's the first one.
He didn't say it mean. He said it like a man reading a gauge he didn't care for, and then he sat and waited to see what she'd do with the pen.
A. Tell Yates she's logging tonight, and his two nights go in by seven.
B. Write tonight's entry true, and not say a word to Yates about it.
C. Leave tonight out, and go check the pump herself every hour till seven.
D. Call Gene at home now and tell him about all three nights.

I'm writing tonight's, Leon. All of it. He looked at the pen a while. She told him the other two nights weren't hers. She hadn't seen them, and she wasn't going to write them for him. They go in the book before Gene reads it at seven. If they're not there, I'll tell him I knew. Yates said she was a pain in the neck, and there wasn't much behind it. At twenty to seven he sat down at the far end of the desk and wrote two short lines under hers, with dates, and went home without saying good night, which for Yates was about normal.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Integrity, with a lead who runs that desk. Your own record you write true, whoever asks you not to. His nights are his to write, and you tell him so to his face with a time on it, before you'd carry them anywhere else. You didn't go over his head at half past three, and you didn't sign up to keep it for him. What would that book have said the night nobody caught it?

On Tuesday she slept till two, and at seven she was on Cedar Street at the brick ranch with the dead hedge. The porch light was on. Down the hall the television was going, low, the way it always was. On the drive over she'd thought about Yates in the chair beside hers at half past three, asking her to leave one night out of the book. She'd been leaving one out for seven years.

Vern had the reading book open to where they'd stopped and the egg timer beside it. She didn't sit. She took the sheet out of her coat and unfolded it on the yellow table and pressed the creases flat with the side of her hand, and he let her do all of that without a word.
Air Force Officer Qualifying Test. Test date, nineteen October, twenty nineteen. Pilot, nineteen. CSO, forty four. Verbal, seventy one. Quantitative, thirty eight. Academic Aptitude, fifty five.
The sheet is on the table between them. How should Kit start?
A. Slide it across, let him read it, and wait for him to ask.
B. Tell him Boyd asked her to stay that winter, then give him the number.
C. Tell him the old scores stand anyway, so none of it matters much now.
D. Say the number first, then the story she told everybody about it.

Pilot came back nineteen. You need twenty five. She said the rest standing up, with her coat still on. Boyd asked me to stay for the inspection that winter. He really asked. I said yes because yes was easier than saying nineteen out loud. She kept her eyes on the sheet. Then I let the shop have it. My mother. Graham. Boyd worst of all. He's spent seven years thinking he cost me something, and I let him. Vern read the sheet top to bottom, every line. Then he put one finger under PILOT. Instrument Comprehension? Ran out of time. I guessed the last nine. He nodded like that was a number he could use, and pointed at the other chair, and she sat.

Right. Log it. Integrity, the hard kind, with nobody making you. The fact first, then your own part, and nobody else's name standing in front of it. Most people open with the reason, and the reason's the part I'd have listened to least. On the test too, the option that owns the miss before it explains it is usually the one they're after.

He didn't say anything about the sheet. He got up and poured two coffees from the percolator, though she hadn't asked for one, and sat back down and turned his class ring on his finger, the one worn thin on one side. She'd seen him do it at the diner without knowing she'd noticed.

Spring of seventy three. You know about the gym. I bought this ring the winter before, and wore it to the flight physical so I'd have something to turn. He turned it. Eye chart on the back of a door. I read it right down to the line that counted, and that line came out like somebody'd breathed on it. One line. The flight surgeon wrote one word on my form, and that night I went and looked it up, like the dictionary might've had it wrong.

He took a pencil out of the coffee can and printed it in the margin of her sheet, under her 19, in his capitals. ACUITY. It was the first word anybody had ever written on that page. Closest in meaning, Sergeant.

Sharpness. Sharpness. I had all of it but one line. The navigator school had offered him a seat the same week, he said, and he'd said yes before the man finished asking. He left the word where it was, in the margin under her 19, and she let it stay.

That's the fix I'd have taken. A, C, U is sharp. Acute, acumen, the needle in acupuncture. Acuity is sharpness, mostly of the eye or the mind. When a choice only sounds like the word, or only sits near it, ask which word is actually in front of you. Mine was acuity. I've spelled it right ever since.

So I navigated. Tolliver's tankers till they pulled the seat, and from eighty five on, the rest of the month, I dispatched for a freight outfit in Kansas City. He drank some coffee. Did my dispatcher course in eighty five with a kid from Denver named Walt Herrera, twenty three, best weather head in the room. Thirty one years after that I signed releases for airplanes I never got on. My name went next to the captain's on every one of them.

Kit had the card in her coat too. She'd written it Monday at four in the morning, after the pump came back, in pen on an index card out of the supply drawer at the plant. She took it out and set it face up by his coffee. I WANT TO FLY. It was the sentence from LETTER 2, the one she'd never printed.
Vern read it once. He stood it up against the percolator, where it would be in front of him every time he poured, and went down the hall to the den. He came back with a log out of the box.

My log, twenty seven February, oh one. Tolliver, preflight. Crew chief found fuel weeping at a panel under the left wing. Oh five twenty, counted twelve drops in four minutes. Oh five fifty, counted fifteen drops in three minutes. Crew chief wrote it up. No go. I had the fuel to fly it. Not the question.
She didn't ask whose jet it was.
How much faster was the leak going at the second count?
A. Two drops a minute faster: five a minute against three.
B. Three drops a minute faster: fifteen against twelve.
C. Faster, but she'd want a third count before she said how much.
D. A quarter faster: fifteen is a quarter more than twelve.

Twelve in four minutes is three a minute. Fifteen in three is five. Two a minute faster in half an hour, and still climbing when they quit counting. She looked at his last line a long time. I had the fuel to fly it. Not the question. For seven years she'd let a nineteen answer whether she should fly. Nobody had asked her whether she wanted to. Crew chief was right, Vern said, and that was all he said about that.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Put both counts on the same clock before you compare them. Per minute, per hour, per anything, as long as it's the same per. Fifteen looks like a little more than twelve until you notice it got there a minute quicker. And here's what that crew chief taught me. I could work out what the leak would cost us in fuel, to the pound. That arithmetic answered a question nobody'd asked.
Decision eight. The coat on the hook.

Graham was at the kitchen table on Orchard Street with a stack of lab reports and a red pen when she got home at half past nine. He'd left the porch light on and the radio off. Behind him on the fridge he'd boxed off Saturday, April 3, in green: PRACTICE TEST, 5 HRS, ME ON THE CLOCK.
On Saturday she'd told him all of the wheel, her own part in it too, standing at that counter. That had been hard. This one she'd been carrying a lot longer.

She hung her coat on the hook by the door with the sheet still in the inside pocket. He looked up from a sophomore's graph and took her in, the coat and the hook and her face. You look like he made you do long division for two hours straight. How was Vern tonight?
A. Tell him Vern was fine, and leave the coat where it hangs.
B. Tell him it's the same old Boyd story, and ask about his week.
C. Tell him a part of 2019 is hers, and give him a day.
D. Tell him Vern guessed she'd sat the test before, and leave it there.

There's a part of 2019 you haven't heard. It's mine. It isn't Boyd's. Graham put the red pen down on the graph. Do you want to tell me now? Not tonight. Tonight it'd come out as Boyd's story with a different ending. Saturday the third, after the practice test. All of it, with the paper on the table. Okay. It came right away this time, no beat in front of it. Then she heard what she'd said. After the practice test. Nine years of afters, and she'd just handed him one more, and he'd taken it the way he took all the others. Before he went up to bed he took the marker off the fridge and wrote 2019 in the square for Saturday, April 3, small, in his own black.

Right. Log it. Communication. You didn't hand him all of it, and you didn't let him think there was nothing to hand. He knows it's there, he knows whose it is, and he knows when he gets it. In my trade a release has a time on it, and nobody slides it. You named the time. Now you owe it.
Decision nine. The ten gallon line.
At Monday's huddle Gene read all three lines, hers and Yates's two under it, and didn't make a speech about any of them. He ordered a valve before lunch.

Her next stretch of nights started at eleven Wednesday night. There was a note taped to the pump in Gene's square printing: DEGAS VALVE ORDERED. CHECK THE HEAD EVERY HOUR TILL IT COMES. At three Thursday morning she did the check.

Then she read the drum. At eleven, when she came on, the sight tube had said 50 gallons. Now it said 46. The plant changed drums at 10, never lower, because the bottom of a drum was where the worst of it settled. Day shift would want to know when to have the next one on the dolly.
When will the drum be down to its ten gallon line?
A. Saturday at 1 AM: all forty six gallons at a gallon an hour.
B. Friday at 11 AM: thirty six hours from eleven Wednesday night.
C. Friday at 3 PM: thirty six gallons at a gallon an hour.
D. Thursday at 1 PM: the ten gallons at a gallon an hour.

Fifty to forty six in four hours is a gallon an hour, twenty four a day, same as the log said. Forty six less the ten she couldn't use is thirty six. Thirty six gallons at one an hour is thirty six hours, and three Thursday morning plus thirty six hours is three Friday afternoon. She wrote CHANGE DRUM FRI 1500 on the board by the door and put her initials after it.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Three steps, and each one feeds the next. Get the rate from the two readings, take off what you can't use, then divide and add it to the clock from where you're standing. Four gallons in four hours is one an hour. Thirty six above the line is thirty six hours. The step people skip is the floor, the ten gallons nobody's allowed to pull.
The next Tuesday the card was still standing against the percolator.

This one I can't teach you. He laid a typed page on the table. Twenty statements, each with a row of five boxes, strongly disagree on one end and strongly agree on the other. None of these came off the test. I wrote them at this table Sunday. The real one's two hundred forty in forty five minutes, and nobody grades it, and nobody can tell you what to put. Eleven seconds a line. He cranked the egg timer to four.

She went fast. I like to know the plan before I start. Moderately agree. I'd rather fix a thing myself than ask for help. Strongly agree. I stay calm when things go wrong. Moderately agree. Then number eleven. When I want something, I say so.
Her pencil was in the moderately agree box before she'd read to the end, the way your hand finds the light switch in your own kitchen. Then it stopped there.
It's number eleven, and the egg timer's running. How should she answer it?
A. Stop and think it through until she's sure she has it right.
B. Mark what's true of her today, the first honest answer, and go on.
C. Mark what a good officer candidate would say, and keep going.
D. Skip it, and come back to it if there's time at the end.

She moved the pencil two boxes over and marked moderately disagree. It took about two seconds. For seven years she'd described herself as the crew chief who stayed, and she'd described her well, and it had been the wrong woman. She did the last nine fast. When the timer rang, Vern turned the page face down without reading a word of it. Those are yours.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Nothing to get right on that one. It isn't graded, and in the 2015 pamphlet it feeds no composite. Answer as you are today, quick, and the same way you'd answer it on any other day. The people who do it badly are the ones trying to work out what each line is for. Guessing what they want makes you slower, and it makes you somebody you aren't.
After that he set the night's arithmetic, ten problems in his capitals, and she did them on the egg timer.

A receiver came onto the boom needing 21,000 pounds. For the first six minutes the boom passed fuel at 2,500 pounds a minute. Then the receiver's tanks started to fill, the flow slowed to 1,500 pounds a minute, and it stayed there to the end.
Underneath, in his capitals: HOW LONG ON THE BOOM. He'd underlined LONG.
A. Ten and a half minutes, at the average of the two rates.
B. Fourteen minutes, all of it at the slow rate.
C. Eight minutes twenty four seconds, all of it at the fast rate.
D. Ten minutes: six fast, then four slow.

Six minutes at twenty five hundred is fifteen thousand. That leaves six thousand at fifteen hundred a minute, four minutes more. Ten. She wrote it and circled it. Vern looked at the circle, then up at the stove clock. Nine already. He said that would do for one night.

Right. Log it. When the rate changes partway, cut the problem where it changes and work each piece. Averaging two rates only works when each one ran the same length of time, and these didn't. Six minutes fast, four slow. Every boom operator I ever flew with said the last few thousand pounds take the longest, and none of them was ever wrong about it.

At the front door that night the television down the hall went quiet, and a small woman came out of there. Short white hair, reading glasses shoved up on her head, a pie in a glass dish under a dish towel.

You're the sergeant. I'm Patrice. It's gooseberry. I froze them in June, and he'll eat the whole thing standing up if it stays in this house. She put it in Kit's hands. Then she looked back toward the kitchen. Vern had the water running over the cups and was pretending he couldn't hear. He hasn't talked this much in years. He won't tell me what about, which is how I know it's yours. She tipped her head at the percolator. And that card's been against my coffee pot a week. He moves it to pour and puts it back.

On Saturday, March 20, Kit brought the dish back washed, to the heritage room, because she knew he'd be there. Nobody had wandered in. He had the reading book open on the cleared table, and he shoved the egg timer over so the dish had somewhere to go.
Graham had a date. It was on the whiteboard in his black marker, 2019 in the square for April 3, and she saw it every morning when she got the milk out.
She hadn't come about the dish.
What should she ask Vern to keep?
A. Ask him to keep it till she's told Graham and Boyd herself.
B. Ask him to keep it until after the test in May.
C. Ask him to tell the Lieutenant about 2019 before somebody else can.
D. Ask him to keep 2019 between the two of them, for good.
Keep it till I've told Graham and Boyd myself. Graham first. Then ask me if I did. Vern let her get all the way to the end of it. I can ask.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity, with some Communication in it. You didn't ask him to carry it for you or to bury it. You asked him to hold it while you deliver it yourself, in order, to the people it belongs to, and you gave him leave to check on you. The test likes that shape too: you own the job, and you let somebody hold you to it.
Vern looked at the pie dish for a while. Patrice's dish, washed, with the dish towel folded on top of it the way Patrice had sent it.
It isn't mine to tell, Sergeant. He moved the dish an inch, for no reason. And it isn't yours to keep forever.

Then he dug in the corduroy jacket, the one from the diner in January, and came up with a log folded once. He gave her logs on Tuesdays, at the end of the night, picked for the week's work. This wasn't a Tuesday, and he didn't say what it was for. He held it out across the table anyway.
Kit took it and didn't open it. It rode home on the passenger seat, under her right hand at every stop sign on the river road.
